column2: Their business was settled, but they were still in the mood for drinking. Hu had always been interested in pawnshops, and this was a good opportunity to learn. “Brother Funian,” he began, “did you start out in the pawnbroking trade?” “No, but I know something about it. My late third uncle was a pawnshop appraiser, and I lived with him for a year.” Zhu went on to describe many of the trade’s rules and abuses, speaking so engagingly that Hu heard one thing after another entirely new to him. At last, with something between a sigh and an expression of regret, he said, “I never entered the trade. Even now I cannot tell whether that was a wise decision or a mistake. Earning your living in a pawnshop is unlike any other occupation. Of all the three hundred and sixty trades, it is the most comfortable: good accommodation, good food, generous pay, and light work. Once you have eaten from that bowl, it is hard to stomach any other.” “From what you say, finding good staff to open a pawnshop cannot be easy. An able man who gets on well with his employer is better off staying where he is. He will not readily take another position. Is that right?” “Broadly speaking, yes. But new talent keeps emerging. Sometimes there is no room for advancement in a man’s own shop, and he seeks an opportunity elsewhere.” “Then keep an eye out for me. I should like to meet someone of that sort.” Clearly Hu was considering opening a pawnshop himself. Zhu readily agreed and seemed eager to try his hand, treating his partial knowledge as full expertise and making up for the opportunity he had missed in his youth.

Zhu met Gilbert the next day, just as Chen Shunsheng was enquiring about the shipping space and a demand had arrived from the London head office, forwarded by the East India Company, asking why this year’s silk had still not been shipped. The moment Gilbert saw him, he asked whether Hengji’s and Yuji’s consignments had left Shanghai. “The boats sail tomorrow,” Zhu replied in English. “Mr Gilbert, I feel a moral obligation towards you. I must try to secure one last opportunity for you. There has been important news in the business world lately. Have you heard it?” “I do not know what you mean.” “Hengji’s proprietor, my employer Mr Pang, has entered into a business partnership with Hu Xueyan. Hu’s resources were insufficient, but he is a most unusual figure in business. Above all, he has excellent connections in every quarter and is exceptionally resourceful. Those are his greatest assets. What he lacked was cash, and his partnership with Mr Pang has fully remedied that deficiency. I can therefore say this: Hu Xueyan is invincible. No one can defeat him in business, including you, Mr Gilbert.” “I have no need to defeat him. I am concerned only with my company’s interests. It was your advice I followed in the first place. Otherwise we should never have reached this impasse.” Zhu’s face hardened. “Mr Gilbert, do you wish to discuss who is responsible?” “No.” Gilbert shook his head. “That would serve no purpose. I cannot demand compensation from you, so what is the point of talking about responsibility? Your feeling of moral obligation shows that you still have some friendship for me. I hope we remain friends.”

Zhu responded with a look of sincerity. “That is precisely why I want to do what friendship requires.” He paused, then continued in a calm but firm voice. “Mr Gilbert, you have not been defeated. Everything can still go according to your original plan. But if you miss this final opportunity, your failure will extend beyond this one occasion, into next year and the years that follow. To put it simply, you will be unable to buy the silk you need in Shanghai.” “Do you think the price could be reduced at all?” Gilbert asked. “If you can arrange that, we shall of course pay you the commission you deserve.” “No!” Zhu was emphatic. “It is absolutely impossible. You should know that Hu Xueyan’s shrewdness in business is unequalled. He is already being very generous in not claiming compensation for the losses caused by the delay.” “Very well.” Gilbert finally yielded. “I agree to everything. I ask only that we sign the contract quickly.”

Once the contract was signed, payment collected, and the silk delivered, Hu felt a great weight lift from him. Yet after a whole night’s calculations he was left strangely empty, scarcely knowing for whom he had worked and worried so hard. The profit was indeed a hundred and eighty thousand taels, but it only sounded impressive: not even a handsome figure on paper survived. There were too many partners and too many expenses. The profits had to be shared with You Laowu and Gu Yingchun, and then with Yu Si. Interest had to be paid in various quarters; Wang Youling’s deficit at the Sea Transport Bureau had to be made good; Qiu Fengyan and Ji Heling also had to receive their tokens of appreciation. That left very little. There were still the outstanding bills from his three households in Hangzhou, Huzhou, and Tongli. A close reckoning showed that, apart from the capital of Fukang Bank, which remained entirely a debt, he was another ten thousand taels or so short. Ten thousand taels in itself did not worry him. What troubled him was that so much thought and effort should end in a deficit. If that was how he meant to build a business, was he not climbing a tree to catch fish? It ought not to have worked out this way. There must be a reason, some fault in his own methods. Until he found it, he could neither eat nor sleep in peace. Although he had been awake all night and his head was heavy, a peculiar nervous excitement kept him from wanting to go to bed.

Towards noon, Gu Yingchun and Liu Bucai came together. The moment Gu saw him, he exclaimed, “Little Uncle, you look dreadful! Are you ill?” Liu had once run a pharmacy and could diagnose such ordinary ailments as colds and fevers. He felt Hu’s forehead, asked him to put out his tongue, examined its coating, and gave a very accurate diagnosis. “Too little sleep and too much mental exertion. Deficiency heat is rising. Eat a good meal and have a comfortable sleep, and you will feel yourself again.” “Exactly.” Hu deliberately found a reason to send him away. “Please arrange for me to meet Pang somewhere this evening. Come and find me at Yudechi Bathhouse at four or five.” Once Liu had left, Hu brought out the individual statements he had calculated beforehand and handed Gu his. According to Hu’s reckoning, Gu was entitled to a profit of more than fifteen thousand taels. Gu glanced through it and pushed it back. “Little Uncle, first, you have allotted me too much. Second, let us make no distribution now. We shall go on working together. What matters is to discuss how we should proceed.” “That is precisely what I do not know!” Hu blurted out, frowning and shaking his head repeatedly. His strange manner startled Gu. With some difficulty, he said, “Little Uncle, you seem to have some trouble you find hard to speak about. We are all friends. Tell me what you need. If there is anything you cannot settle, leave my share out of the reckoning.”

Deeply moved, Hu answered frankly, “Brother Yingchun, I have gained nothing—except the loyalty and affection of friends, which a fortune could never buy.” “Worth more than any fortune! But do not say you have gained nothing, Little Uncle. To my mind you have gained a great deal. Take Zhu Funian alone. Pang has something of a pampered young gentleman’s temper and sometimes speaks without sparing anyone’s feelings, but he is generous to his staff in a way few employers are. Yet Zhu still harboured disloyal intentions. Only when he encountered you did an enemy become a friend and submit completely. That is your great ability and your great capital.” These observations went to the heart of the matter; they were far more than empty compliments. Hu was greatly encouraged. “Old Gu,” he asked outright, “speak frankly. What faults do you see in the way I do business? What should I change?”

“I would not call them faults. But there is a Chinese saying: ‘A calling is mastered through diligence and ruined by play.’ I take ‘diligence’ to mean respect for one’s calling. And ‘play’, in turn, means not laziness but a shallow lack of seriousness. Respect brings concentration; single-minded concentration brings continual improvement. Little Uncle, if you have made a mistake, I must tell you plainly that it is a lack of concentration. A man’s energy is limited, after all, and you have far too many affairs in hand. For the moment, everything seems to be attended to and nothing has gone wrong. Yet who can say how many good opportunities you may have missed?” Hu nodded throughout. When Gu had finished, he immediately replied, “Several people have advised me along these lines, but none has explained it as clearly as you. Just now I was thinking that after all this effort I was left empty-handed. There must be something wrong. You say I lack concentration. That is my fault. Still, I cannot really say I am empty-handed…” He stopped, afraid that saying more might make Gu uneasy. He himself had nothing to show for his work and was even in debt, but all the friends who had worked with him had benefited. Viewed from that side of the ledger, he had achieved something after all.

The thought revived him further. “Come, come!” He rose. “We shall follow Third Master Liu’s advice: a good meal and a good sleep. Is there any good Western food to be had? Afterwards we can spend the afternoon soaking at Yudechi.” “There is, but I am afraid you might not like it.” “Why should I not?” “In summer the fashionable thing is a se-bai Western dinner: cold, lightly flavoured food, raw or only half cooked. It can turn your stomach if you are not used to it.” “Then forget it. We had better…” “We had better eat at my place. Seventh Sister has returned to simpler ways. She is learning to cook from everyone she meets. Today she is making chicken steamed with rice meal, and there is water shield from your own West Lake…” “Say no more!” Hu swallowed. “If you go on, I shall start drooling.” They went together to Gu’s house. Sure enough, the Seventh Lady had rolled up her sleeves and was busy in the kitchen. The heat had brought a sheen of perspiration to her round, silver-basin face and her lotus-root arms, making their pink and white all the more vivid. Seeing Hu peer through the kitchen doorway, she called at once, “It is like the Flaming Mountain in here! Do not come in, Little Uncle!” “I am hungry,” he replied honestly. “Whatever you have, give me something to eat first.” “I shall cook a bowl of rice noodles to take the edge off your hunger. Then we can have a leisurely drink.” He finished a bowl of rice noodles in chicken broth with ham and dried bamboo shoots, and the table was set for wine. You Laowu happened to arrive as well, putting Hu in still better spirits.

Naturally they asked about his plans, but he put the question back to You and Gu: what course would benefit everyone? “That is difficult to say,” You replied. “If I had my way, you would leave everyone else’s affairs alone.” “Just listen to Brother Five!” The Seventh Lady was direct by nature and at once supplied the words he had left unsaid. “Leave everyone else’s affairs alone and attend only to yours. Is that it?” Everyone laughed. “Of course that is only wishful thinking on my part,” You said. Then he grew serious. “But the ways of earning a living are narrowing for our grain-transport brotherhoods. You promised, Little Uncle. You must find a way for us.” “Certainly, certainly. I shall treat it as my own business.” Hu turned to Gu. “And what do you think I should do?” “I told you just now.” Hu nodded, recalling the advice Gu had given him that morning. You and the Seventh Lady had not heard it. Impatient as ever, she pressed him for an explanation, and he repeated Gu’s counsel about concentrating his efforts, warmly praising its insight and clarity.

“Thanks to him and his entire family!” The Seventh Lady curled her lip. “Little Uncle, he is a bungling strategist. Do not listen to him.” Gu disagreed but dared not argue with her. He merely said, “Little Uncle, ‘Take care never to heed a woman’s words.’” “What do you mean, ‘a woman’s words’?” she retorted instantly. “Surely the larger your sphere of activity, the better. By your reasoning, a man should refuse to be emperor because he would have too many different affairs to manage!” That left Gu without an answer. He shook his head and murmured, “Eighteen varieties of crooked reasoning.” Hu was amused by Gu’s helpless embarrassment. You, however, who usually took a dim view of his precious younger sister, now supported her. “What Seventh Sister says is not altogether unreasonable. There is no harm in having many affairs, provided there are people to manage them. Being emperor is easy; the difficulty is finding a good chief minister. Little Uncle, I think Old Gu is right, but Seventh Sister’s comparison also makes sense. You are a clever man. Think over what they have both said and work out a plan.” “Yes.” Hu nodded gravely. As he ate, drank, and chatted, he kept turning the matter over. By the time he had enjoyed enough wine and food, his plan was largely settled.

“Brother Five, Old Gu,” he began, “first let us divide up the accounts…” “There is no need!” You interrupted. His view was the same as Gu’s: the original capital and the profits should remain entirely at Hu’s disposal, to earn profit upon profit. “I understand,” Hu said. “But I want to make a fresh start, with several businesses managed separately by different people, while I take overall charge. Like an emperor, I shall have ministers handling their own affairs without needing to do everything myself.” All three listeners nodded their agreement. “First comes banking. That is my foundation, and I know the trade, so I shall probably still have to attend to it myself. Second comes silk. In Huzhou I shall put Chen Shilong in charge; in Shanghai, Old Gu.” “Good,” Gu replied. “I shall accept that responsibility without standing on ceremony. Later we can also export tea and tung oil. We can discuss those in due course.” “All our exports will be in your hands. I have thought about tea and tung oil too. If you think they are worth doing, I shall support you. But the new silk will soon be on the market, so you must begin planning at once. Concentrate entirely on that and leave everything else alone. Except…” He glanced at the Seventh Lady and stopped with a smile.

There was plainly something behind the remark, and the Seventh Lady could not help asking, “Except what, Little Uncle?” “Except,” Hu answered, laughing, “that however much you leave everything else alone, your marriage must be attended to. The same goes for me. I can no longer concern myself with every other matter, but I must see this one through for you. With Brother Five here, let me say this as your chief matchmaker: choose a day and arrange the wedding. The bride’s and bridegroom’s families can discuss it directly without having me carry messages between them. I shall bring the Gu family’s old clan head round. I am certain it can be done, so set your minds at rest.” “Yes,” You said, nodding. “We must have a proper talk about it in the next few days. But let us leave it for now. Go on with your plans, Little Uncle.”

“I also intend to start two other businesses: a pawnshop and a pharmacy. I shall ask Third Master Liu to run the pharmacy. As for the pawnshop, I want to speak to Pang and ask for Zhu Funian’s help.” You and Gu offered neither approval nor objection. Their silence meant that they did not agree. Gu thought Hu should not enter trades he did not understand. Liu Bucai’s temperament was also ill suited to the hard work of establishing a new business. As for Zhu, they had known him only a short time. Though they might now say of him, “The southern barbarians will never rebel again,” his actual abilities were still uncertain. How could such important responsibilities be entrusted to him so readily? You had similar thoughts and another doubt besides, which he expressed frankly. “Little Uncle, banking needs a great deal of capital, and so does silk. Where will you find the means to open a pawnshop and a pharmacy as well?” “Brother Five has put his finger on the point,” Hu said eagerly. “Naturally I have made plans.” His plan was to use his reputation and ability to enlist other people’s help. Pang had promised support for a Fukang branch, while the silk business would continue to be financed by pooled shares. For the pawnshop’s capital, he had his eye on Pan Shuya and the other wealthy young gentlemen of Suzhou. For the pharmacy, he intended to find a way through official circles in Jiangsu and Zhejiang.

“Let me explain why I want a pawnshop and a pharmacy. Neither will make a profit immediately. I mean them entirely for the public good. A pawnshop will help poor people. Quite a few people already know the name Hu Xueyan, but they are all officials and businessmen. In future I want ordinary people to know it too. When they hear my name, I want them to say, ‘That is a decent man!’ Then my businesses will keep growing. That is why I want a pharmacy: it is the best way to make a name. Besides, troubled times bring illness, and great upheavals are always followed by epidemics. A pharmacy will benefit others and ourselves. It is one of the best businesses there is.” The Seventh Lady was the first to express her admiration. “Listen to him,” she told Gu, with a touch of admonition. “That is real foresight! Little Uncle is already looking beyond the war. You ought to learn from him.” “I am learning from him.” Gu turned to Hu. “You said the pharmacy’s capital would come from public funds. How would that work?” “Through our connections. The army must have medicines. I shall discuss it with Third Master Liu and get a couple of good prescriptions, then prepare them properly with genuine ingredients—wound medicine, for instance, Zhuge Marching Powder, or Biwen Pills. They must work with a single dose and stand apart from ordinary remedies. Then we can ask the various army supply offices to place advance orders and use their payments as capital.” The Seventh Lady was delighted. “Really! I do not believe there is anything in the world Little Uncle cannot find a way to do!” Hu was a little alarmed. “Seventh Sister, that is far too much praise. A single man’s strength is limited. Even with three heads and six arms, how much could he do? Great undertakings depend entirely on people working together. You might say I have nothing except friends. Only if you treat your friends’ affairs as your own will they treat yours as theirs. Without friends, the greatest ability in the world will still get you nowhere.”

“You have struck the nail on the head, Little Uncle,” You said at once. “All our brothers regard you as a good friend. They are waiting for your orders.” “Not so fast! I promised to find a livelihood for you, and I shall keep that promise. To tell you the truth, opening that path is my most urgent business. I already have the outline of a plan…” This was another major undertaking affecting both the people’s livelihood and the country’s economy. Hu intended to use the grain-transport brotherhoods’ manpower, influence along the waterways, and existing boats to carry government and private cargo. At the same time, he would use the Songjiang brotherhood’s Tongyu Rice Shop as the basis for a large grain business. “There are several reasons why rice costs as much as pearls and firewood as much as cassia in wartime. We must examine them one by one. Fighting leaves fields untended and reduces production: that is one reason. Another is the difficulty of transport. How wasteful it is when places have rice but cannot move it out or sell it! But there is something more wasteful still: grain destroyed outright. Some households have large stores, only to see them burned in the fighting. Or autumn comes and the war draws near: rice stands ready in the fields, but there is no one to cut it, and it is wasted. If we could prevent that waste, think what a benefit it would be to the public and to ourselves!” “That makes sense!” You sprang up. “I understand the first two reasons, but I have never heard this last point made before. Tell me, Little Uncle, how can we prevent the waste?” “By watching the situation. We must see clearly and act quickly. When a place is becoming unsafe, we send plenty of boats and get its stored grain out in time. Any rice ready for cutting must be harvested quickly too. Of course we shall need official help: troops to protect us, perhaps, or special accommodation at the checkpoints. Once it is all arranged, Brother Five, you will have both the cooperation of your people and the advantages of the waterways. No one else could match the business.”

You and Gu were silent. They considered Hu’s words carefully before grasping the broad outline of his method. It was indeed an excellent business that no one else could wrest from them, but carrying it out would not be easy. “You know how officials are, Little Uncle. They may not be willing to help.” “They certainly will! It all depends on how the case is put. There is another reason: war requires two things, troops and grain—enough food and enough soldiers. There is only so much grain, and both sides are in the same area. Every measure we gain is one the Taipings lose. The effect on both sides is considerable. Once I explain that, the authorities are bound to approve.” “Exactly!” You asked, “Whom do you intend to speak to? Prefect Wang?” “Yes, I shall speak to him first. There is no time to lose. I leave tomorrow! I have plenty of other ways to deal with the Taipings, such as tightening the suppression of smuggling and cutting off their supplies of everyday necessities.” Hu stood up and waved his hand with enthusiasm. “Small traders adapt themselves to circumstances. A businessman on a large scale first helps the government change the circumstances. Once the overall situation improves, our business will find its way. Just wait. When I reach Hangzhou, I shall make a fresh start and launch undertakings that will really stir the world.”
End of this part.

By this point, Hu Xueyan has relied on official support, made use of the grain-transport brotherhoods, established connections with foreign merchants and compradors, recruited gamblers, and cultivated wealthy businessmen. He has at last risen to prosperity in an age of war, establishing himself in Shanghai and Hangzhou.

In The Red-Topped Merchant, Towers of Light, and other books, Gao Yang continues to draw on his extensive historical knowledge and accomplished storytelling to recount how Hu Xueyan’s wealth rose to its height after his beginnings in Shanghai and Hangzhou, and how he ultimately went bankrupt. These books describe Hu, by then a great merchant of Jiangsu and Zhejiang, transporting military funds and grain to help the Qing forces relieve the siege of Hangzhou. After the city falls, he turns to Zuo Zongtang as his patron, raising military funds, buying and transporting modern Western guns and artillery, borrowing immense sums from foreign merchants to support Zuo’s western campaigns, and assisting in his Western-style enterprises. Relying on official patronage, Hu then expands his power and comes to dominate commerce in Jiangsu and Zhejiang. His reputation spreads throughout the southeast. He is eventually granted the insignia of the second official rank and the privileges of wearing a yellow riding jacket and riding a horse inside the Forbidden City, becoming the only merchant of the late Qing to wear the red-topped official hat. Extravagant in the extreme and passionately fond of women, he builds splendid residences and gardens in Shanghai, Hangzhou, and elsewhere, surrounds himself with concubines, and delights in unrestrained debauchery. For more than a decade, his wealth and influence reach extraordinary heights. Yet Hu does not possess truly remarkable strategy or far-reaching ability. Unable to withstand the pressure of foreign merchants, his business gradually declines. Prosperity turns to ruin, until he is bankrupt and his reputation destroyed. He thus becomes one of the singular figures of China’s modern history.

With a distinctive eye and an inspired pen, Gao Yang creates intricate plots, lifelike characters, fluent prose, and scenes of great scope, bringing a vivid picture of the turbulent society of the late Qing to the page.

For the story of how Hu Xueyan, the great merchant of the late Qing, moved from commerce into official rank and rose and fell with such dramatic speed, see The Red-Topped Merchant, Towers of Light, and other titles published by our company.
